note.explanation: Ionic compounds consist of oppositely charged ions held together by strong electrostatic forces. Covalent compounds mostly consist of neutral molecules, with shared electrons attracting the nuclei. These different structures help explain how the compounds melt, dissolve and conduct electricity.
examples: Sodium chloride is an ionic compound with a high melting point (801°C).
Covalent compounds are usually poor conductors of electricity.
note.checkAnswer: Ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten or dissolved because they have free ions that can move.
note.simple: Ionic compounds have charged ions; covalent compounds mostly have neutral molecules. Their different particles explain many of their properties.

written.text: Why does iodine exist as a solid while Cl₂ exist as a gas?
written.finalAnswer: Iodine molecules are larger and have greater molecular mass than Cl₂ molecules, so the attractions between iodine molecules are stronger. More energy is needed to separate them, so iodine is solid while Cl₂ is a gas.

written.text: Compare the properties of ionic and covalent compounds.
written.finalAnswer: Ionic compounds have oppositely charged ions arranged in a crystalline structure, while covalent compounds mostly exist as discrete neutral molecules. Ionic compounds usually have high melting and boiling points; covalent compounds generally have lower melting and boiling points. Ionic compounds are generally soluble in polar solvents like water, while covalent compounds are usually insoluble in water but soluble in non-polar solvents. Ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten or in solution because they have free ions; covalent compounds are usually bad conductors.

example.question: Compare the properties of ionic and covalent compounds.
example.answer: Ionic compounds have oppositely charged ions arranged in a crystalline structure and usually have high melting and boiling points. They are generally soluble in polar solvents and conduct electricity when molten or in solution because they have free ions. Covalent compounds mostly exist as discrete neutral molecules, generally have lower melting and boiling points, are usually insoluble in water but soluble in non-polar solvents, and are usually bad conductors.

explain.title: Ionic compounds
explain.body: In ionic compounds oppositely charged ions are properly arranged to give a crystalline structure. As a whole the compound is neutral. There exists a strong electrostatic force between their ions. Ionic compounds are usually solids with high melting and boiling points. They are generally soluble in polar solvents like water and conduct electricity when molten or in solution because free ions are present.

explain.title: Covalent compounds
explain.body: Covalent compounds mostly exist as discrete neutral molecules. There exists a strong electrostatic attraction between the nuclei and the shared electrons. Lower molecular mass covalent compounds are gases or low-boiling liquids, while high molecular mass covalent compounds exist as solids. They generally have lower melting and boiling points, are usually insoluble in water but soluble in non-polar solvents, and are usually bad conductors of electricity.

explain.title: Use the particle explanation
explain.body: When explaining a property, connect it to the particles. For example, ionic compounds conduct electricity in the molten state or in solution because they contain free ions. Do not confuse this with solid ionic compounds, where the ions are held in the crystal arrangement.

mistakes: Saying ionic compounds conduct electricity as solids; the section says they conduct when molten or in solution.
Forgetting to explain that free ions are responsible for ionic conductivity.
Claiming that every covalent compound is a gas or liquid; high molecular mass covalent compounds can be solids.
Reversing the usual solubility patterns: ionic compounds are generally soluble in polar solvents, while covalent compounds are usually soluble in non-polar solvents.
Writing only one side of a comparison question instead of comparing both ionic and covalent compounds.
